answer:
Both symptoms are the notification channel: on Android 8+ a notification posted to a channel that was never created is dropped silently, and a channel's behaviour is frozen the moment it is first created.

Every notification carries a channel id — it is the first argument of `NotificationCompat.Builder(context, channelId)`. If no channel with that id exists, `notify()` is a no-op and logcat prints `No Channel found for pkg=...`. Nothing throws. Create your channels in `Application.onCreate`: `createNotificationChannel` is idempotent, so calling it on every launch costs nothing.

### What the user owns
- Per channel, not per app: importance, sound, vibration, light, badge, lock-screen visibility, and blocking it outright. That is the whole point — the user mutes "Promotions" and keeps "Delivery updates".
- `areNotificationsEnabled()` is the app-level switch. A single channel can be blocked while that still returns true, so read `getNotificationChannelCompat(id)?.importance == IMPORTANCE_NONE` before you conclude anything.
- You can deep-link into one channel's settings with `Settings.ACTION_CHANNEL_NOTIFICATION_SETTINGS`, which beats dumping the user in a generic screen.

### What you can still change
- Name, description and group are updated by a repeat `createNotificationChannel` call.
- Importance, sound, vibration, lights and badge are not. Re-creating the channel with new values is ignored.
- Deleting and re-creating the same id restores the user's old settings, and Settings still counts the deleted channels. To genuinely change behaviour you ship a new id — `delivery_v2` — and delete the old one.

Treat channels as a product decision, not plumbing: a handful of categories named for what a user would want to mute.

The white square is your full-colour launcher icon reduced to its alpha channel, and the dead tap is a missing `setContentIntent` — neither is an error the build will catch.

### The pieces a notification actually needs
- A **channel id**, passed to `NotificationCompat.Builder(context, id)`. There is no default channel.
- **`setSmallIcon`** — the only genuinely mandatory field; posting a notification without one throws `IllegalArgumentException` at `notify()` time.
- **`setContentTitle`** and **`setContentText`** — this is what the collapsed row shows, with or without a style.
- **`setContentIntent`** — a `PendingIntent` fired on tap, usually with `setAutoCancel(true)` so the row disappears once used.
- `notify(id, notification)` through `NotificationManagerCompat`, which on Android 13+ needs `POST_NOTIFICATIONS`. The id is the notification's identity: posting the same id again updates it in place rather than adding a second row. Pair it with a tag when ids from different features could collide.

### Why the icon is a white blob
The system keeps only the **alpha channel** of the small icon and tints the silhouette itself — with your `setColor` in the shade, and flat white in the status bar. So it must be a white-on-transparent vector, 24x24dp, no background, no padding of its own. The launcher icon is never the right asset: every coloured pixel is opaque, and an opaque square is exactly what you get.

`setLargeIcon` is the optional right-hand image — an avatar or product shot — and is not a fix for the small one. `setPriority` is a compatibility field read only below API 26; on anything modern the channel decides.
code_example:
// res/drawable/ic_stat_order.xml — white paths on transparent, 24x24dp, no background.
// The system throws the colours away and keeps the silhouette, so a launcher icon = white blob.

val open = Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW, "myapp://orders/42".toUri(), ctx, MainActivity::class.java)
val tap = PendingIntent.getActivity(
  ctx, 0, open, PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE or PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT
)

val notification = NotificationCompat.Builder(ctx, CH_DELIVERY)   // 1. channel id, no default
  .setSmallIcon(R.drawable.ic_stat_order)                         // 2. required, or notify() throws
  .setContentTitle("Order #42 shipped")                           // 3. the collapsed row
  .setContentText("Arrives tomorrow before 18:00")
  .setContentIntent(tap)                                          // 4. without it the tap is dead
  .setAutoCancel(true)
  .setColor(ContextCompat.getColor(ctx, R.color.brand))           // tints the silhouette
  .setLargeIcon(courierAvatar)                                    // optional, not a small-icon fix
  .setPriority(NotificationCompat.PRIORITY_DEFAULT)               // only read below API 26
  .build()

// Posting the same id again updates the row in place instead of stacking a duplicate
private const val ORDER_42 = 42

if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT < Build.VERSION_CODES.TIRAMISU ||
    ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(ctx, Manifest.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS)
      == PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED) {
  NotificationManagerCompat.from(ctx).notify(ORDER_42, notification)
}

Android 13 made notifications opt-in: `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` is a runtime permission, denied by default on a new install, while devices that upgraded with your app already installed and notifications enabled were pre-granted it — which is exactly why only new users are missing.

Declare it in the manifest and request it with the Activity Result contract, guarded by `SDK_INT >= TIRAMISU`.

### Who shows the dialog
- Target API 33 or higher and nothing appears until you ask, so the timing is yours.
- Target 32 or lower and the system asks on your behalf the first time the app creates a notification channel — an unexplained dialog on first launch, which people dismiss.
- Ask in context, never on the splash screen: right after the user turns on price alerts, with your own screen explaining what they get. A permission spent on a cold first launch is usually spent for good.

### When the answer is no
- Two refusals and the permission is permanently denied. The launcher then returns denied instantly with no dialog, and the only remaining route is `Settings.ACTION_APP_NOTIFICATION_SETTINGS` with `EXTRA_APP_PACKAGE`.
- Check `areNotificationsEnabled()` before doing work whose only output is a notification, and give that content somewhere else to live — an in-app inbox, a badge, a banner on next launch.
- FCM data messages still reach `onMessageReceived`; only the visible post is dropped. A foreground service still runs — its notification is hidden from the shade but the user sees it in the Task Manager. Media session notifications are exempt.

Notifications are now a feature the user has to want, so treat the request as part of the feature, not as boilerplate at startup.

`PendingIntent` matching ignores extras, so all ten calls handed you the same token, and `FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT` kept rewriting its extras with the newest order id.

A `PendingIntent` is a token you hand to another process — here the system — which fires it later with your app's identity and permissions, even if your process has died. Because the system caches these, `getActivity()` looks for an existing match before creating one.

### Why they collapse into one
- The match is made on request code, plus the intent's action, data `Uri`, MIME type, component and categories. **Extras are not part of the comparison.**
- So ten `Intent(ctx, DetailActivity::class.java).putExtra("orderId", id)` with request code `0` are one PendingIntent wearing ten hats.
- Fix it by making the intent itself distinct: put the identity in the **data** `Uri` — `myapp://orders/42` — which is compared, and which doubles as your deep link. A unique request code per notification also works, but you have to keep those numbers stable to update or cancel later.

### The flags
- `FLAG_IMMUTABLE` or `FLAG_MUTABLE` is mandatory since Android 12 — omit both and the constructor throws. Default to immutable; use mutable only where the system fills the intent in for you, as `RemoteInput` direct reply does.
- `FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT` — keep the existing token, replace its extras. Correct for a notification you keep re-posting under one id.
- `FLAG_CANCEL_CURRENT` — invalidate the old token everywhere it is held, then issue a new one.
- `FLAG_NO_CREATE` — return null instead of creating, which is how you test whether an alarm is already scheduled.

One tappable thing, one PendingIntent, made unique by its data — not by its extras.

That is a notification trampoline, and since Android 12 the system blocks a service or broadcast receiver started by a notification tap from calling `startActivity` — nothing throws, the Activity just never launches.

The pattern was popular because it gave you one place to sit between the tap and the screen: log the open, resolve the route, decide which Activity to send the user to. It was also slow. The tap had to cold-start the process, queue the broadcast and run your code before a single pixel changed, and the delay landed on the most latency-sensitive moment in the app. The system also could not attribute the eventual launch to the notification.

### What you see now
- Apps targeting API 31 or higher: the launch is dropped and logcat prints `Indirect notification activity start (trampoline) from <pkg> blocked`.
- It is not a crash and not a lint error, so it usually surfaces as "notifications do nothing" from QA on a newer device.

### What replaces it
- Point `setContentIntent` at the Activity with `PendingIntent.getActivity`, and put the route in the intent's data `Uri`. The screen starts immediately.
- Do the logging inside the Activity — in `onCreate` and `onNewIntent`, which is where the intent arrives on a `singleTop` entry point. You have strictly more information there than the receiver had, and the analytics call no longer sits between the tap and the pixels.
- A receiver is still the right tool for an action that opens no UI: mark as read, snooze, dismiss, and `setDeleteIntent` for a swipe-away. The ban is on such a component starting an Activity, not on receivers.
- If work must happen before the screen, start the Activity and let it enqueue that work.

The rule: a tap goes straight to a screen, and everything else happens after it is visible.

On Android 8+ only the channel's importance decides how a notification behaves; the other two are a pre-26 fallback and a delivery setting.

### The three knobs, and what each one really controls
- **Channel importance** — the real one. `IMPORTANCE_HIGH` gives a heads-up and a sound, `DEFAULT` sound only, `LOW` a silent row in the shade, `MIN` a collapsed row with no status-bar icon, `NONE` blocked. Set once at creation and owned by the user afterwards, so re-creating the channel with a higher value changes nothing.
- **`setPriority`** — `NotificationCompat` maps it to an importance only below API 26. On a modern device it does not make anything louder; keep it only while your `minSdk` is under 26.
- **FCM message priority** — `high` asks FCM to wake the device out of Doze and deliver now; `normal` may be held until the next maintenance window. It buys latency, not volume. A high-priority push into a `LOW` channel arrives instantly and in silence.

### Why a HIGH channel can still stay quiet
- The user lowered it. Read `getNotificationChannelCompat(id)?.importance` at runtime — that is the ground truth, and it is the first thing to check before rebuilding anything.
- Do Not Disturb is on. Only a channel the user has allowed to bypass DND gets through, and DND filters on `setCategory`, so `CATEGORY_MESSAGE`, `CATEGORY_ALARM` and `CATEGORY_CALL` are worth setting correctly.
- Heads-up also needs the screen on and unlocked, and the system dampens an app that alerts repeatedly in a short window.

Importance is the only volume control you own, and only until the user touches it — everything else is about when the message arrives, not how it lands.

A `NotificationCompat.Style` is what fills the expanded view, and the Conversations section additionally requires `MessagingStyle` plus a long-lived shortcut that the notification points at by id.

Without a style you get one title line and one truncated text line, collapsed and expanded alike. A style only replaces the expanded layout — the collapsed row still comes from `setContentTitle` and `setContentText`, which is why setting `bigText` alone appears to do nothing until the user pulls the notification open.

### The styles worth knowing
- `BigTextStyle` — a readable paragraph. Cheap, and there is rarely a reason not to add it.
- `BigPictureStyle` — one image; `bigLargeIcon(null as Bitmap?)` hides the avatar once expanded, and `showBigPictureWhenCollapsed(true)` shows a thumbnail in the collapsed row. Decode a scaled bitmap off the main thread — the whole notification crosses a Binder transaction.
- `InboxStyle` — up to about six `addLine` entries; mostly superseded by grouping.
- `CallStyle` — `forIncomingCall` / `forOngoingCall`, the supported way to render a call instead of hand-rolled `RemoteViews`.

### What makes it a conversation
1. Publish a long-lived dynamic shortcut for that chat: `ShortcutInfoCompat` with `setLongLived(true)` and a `Person`, pushed via `ShortcutManagerCompat.pushDynamicShortcut`.
2. Build with `MessagingStyle`, adding each message with its own `Person` so the system draws avatars and the chat layout.
3. Call `setShortcutId` with the same id and `setCategory(CATEGORY_MESSAGE)`.

That combination is what unlocks the Conversations section, Priority conversations, bubbles via `setBubbleMetadata`, and per-conversation settings. Miss the shortcut and the notification quietly falls back to the ordinary section.
code_example:
val me = Person.Builder().setName("You").setKey("me").build()
val sender = Person.Builder()
  .setName("Dana").setKey("user:88").setIcon(IconCompat.createWithBitmap(avatar)).build()

// 1. A long-lived dynamic shortcut per conversation — without it there is no Conversations section
val shortcutId = "chat:88"
ShortcutManagerCompat.pushDynamicShortcut(
  ctx,
  ShortcutInfoCompat.Builder(ctx, shortcutId)
    .setLongLived(true)
    .setShortLabel("Dana")
    .setPerson(sender)
    .setIcon(IconCompat.createWithBitmap(avatar))
    .setIntent(Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW, "myapp://chats/88".toUri()))
    .build()
)

// 2 + 3. MessagingStyle, tied back to that shortcut id
val chat = NotificationCompat.Builder(ctx, CH_CHAT)
  .setSmallIcon(R.drawable.ic_stat_chat)
  .setShortcutId(shortcutId)
  .setCategory(NotificationCompat.CATEGORY_MESSAGE)
  .setStyle(
    NotificationCompat.MessagingStyle(me)
      .addMessage("Are you nearby?", earlier, sender)
      .addMessage("Table for two at 8", now, sender)
  )
  .build()

// A long body: the style fills the EXPANDED view, contentText still fills the collapsed row
val release = NotificationCompat.Builder(ctx, CH_NEWS)
  .setSmallIcon(R.drawable.ic_stat_news)
  .setContentTitle("Release 4.2 is out")
  .setContentText("Offline sync, faster search, 40 fixes")   // collapsed
  .setStyle(NotificationCompat.BigTextStyle().bigText(fullChangelog))
  .build()

Post them as a group with one summary and set `setGroupAlertBehavior(GROUP_ALERT_SUMMARY)` on every notification in it, so the children go into the shade silently and only the summary makes a sound.

### The three pieces
1. The same `setGroup(KEY)` on every child notification.
2. One extra notification with that same key and `setGroupSummary(true)`, posted under its own id. That is the collapsed row and the text the user actually reads — `InboxStyle` or a count works well here.
3. `setGroupAlertBehavior(GROUP_ALERT_SUMMARY)` on all of them. Each notification reads the flag for itself: on a child it means "stay silent", on the summary it means "you are the one that alerts". `GROUP_ALERT_CHILDREN` is the mirror image, and the default `GROUP_ALERT_ALL` is your ten buzzes.

### The traps
- Android 7+ auto-bundles four or more notifications from one app, so the shade *looks* grouped without a summary — but every child has already alerted by then. Bundling is cosmetic; the alert behaviour is not.
- Re-posting under an existing id alerts again unless you set `setOnlyAlertOnce(true)`. That is the difference between a progress notification and a pager.
- Cancelling children one at a time can leave an orphaned summary. Count what is left with `activeNotifications` and cancel the summary when the last child goes.
- An app is capped at 50 active notifications; past that the system drops them.

Post one notification per thing the user can act on individually. A sync result is not that — one row saying "12 files synced" beats twelve rows, and it is one buzz instead of ten.
code_example:
private const val GROUP_SYNC = "sync_results"
private const val SUMMARY_ID = 0

fun postSyncResults(ctx: Context, files: List<SyncedFile>) {
  val nm = NotificationManagerCompat.from(ctx)

  files.forEach { file ->
    val child = NotificationCompat.Builder(ctx, CH_SYNC)
      .setSmallIcon(R.drawable.ic_stat_sync)
      .setContentTitle(file.name)
      .setContentText(file.status)
      .setGroup(GROUP_SYNC)
      .setGroupAlertBehavior(NotificationCompat.GROUP_ALERT_SUMMARY)  // this child stays silent
      .build()
    nm.notify(file.id.toInt(), child)
  }

  val summary = NotificationCompat.Builder(ctx, CH_SYNC)
    .setSmallIcon(R.drawable.ic_stat_sync)
    .setContentTitle("${files.size} files synced")
    .setStyle(NotificationCompat.InboxStyle().setSummaryText("Sync"))
    .setGroup(GROUP_SYNC)
    .setGroupSummary(true)                                           // the row that alerts
    .setGroupAlertBehavior(NotificationCompat.GROUP_ALERT_SUMMARY)
    .build()
  nm.notify(SUMMARY_ID, summary)
}

// Dismissing children individually can leave the summary hanging — clean it up
fun onChildDismissed(ctx: Context) {
  val nm = ctx.getSystemService(NotificationManager::class.java)
  val remaining = nm.activeNotifications.count {
    it.notification.group == GROUP_SYNC && it.id != SUMMARY_ID
  }
  if (remaining == 0) nm.cancel(SUMMARY_ID)
}

// Updating one notification in place: without this it buzzes again on every progress step
val progress = NotificationCompat.Builder(ctx, CH_SYNC)
  .setSmallIcon(R.drawable.ic_stat_sync)
  .setOnlyAlertOnce(true)
  .setProgress(100, percent, false)
  .build()

The system leaves the reply field in its sending state until you post an update under that same notification id or cancel it — the reply is not finished when your receiver returns.

### Wiring the action
- A `RemoteInput` carries the typed text; attach it to a `NotificationCompat.Action` and post the notification as usual.
- The action's `PendingIntent` must be `FLAG_MUTABLE`. The system writes the reply into that intent, so an immutable one arrives empty and `RemoteInput.getResultsFromIntent()` returns `null` — the single most common direct-reply bug.
- Send it to a `BroadcastReceiver`, not an Activity: the whole point is handling the reply without opening the app. That is not a trampoline — what Android 12 banned is a receiver launched from a notification turning around and starting an Activity.

### Finishing the reply
1. Read the text with `RemoteInput.getResultsFromIntent(intent)` under the key you built the `RemoteInput` with.
2. Hand the actual send to something that outlives the receiver — WorkManager, or a foreground service — because a `BroadcastReceiver` gets about ten seconds.
3. Re-post under the **same id**: with `MessagingStyle` append the outgoing message, otherwise `setRemoteInputHistory(arrayOf(text))`. The spinner clears and the user sees what they sent.
4. Cancel it only once the send actually succeeded. Cancelling on the tap makes a failed send invisible.

`setAllowGeneratedReplies(true)` with `SEMANTIC_ACTION_REPLY` lets the system offer smart replies and lets Android Auto and Wear read the thread aloud.

Mental model: a notification with an action is a small screen you own. The tap starts a transaction, and the notification is your only place to report how it ended.

A message carrying a `notification` block is drawn by the FCM SDK itself whenever your app is not in the foreground, and your `FirebaseMessagingService` is never called; only a data-only message always reaches `onMessageReceived`.

### What each payload shape does
- **notification only** — foreground: `onMessageReceived` runs, nothing is drawn, you decide. Backgrounded or killed: the system posts it and your code never runs.
- **data only** — `onMessageReceived` runs in both states and you build the notification yourself. This is the only shape that lets you dedupe, decrypt, localise or route.
- **both** — backgrounded, the system draws the `notification` half and drops the `data` half into the extras of the Activity the tap launches; your service is skipped. Foreground, you get one `RemoteMessage` carrying both halves. Same payload, two code paths — that asymmetry is what costs people a day.

### What that breaks
- A counter, a badge update or a "mark delivered" call written inside `onMessageReceived` is silently missing for exactly the users who never open the app.
- The system-drawn notification picks its channel from `android.notification.channel_id`, else the manifest's `default_notification_channel_id` meta-data, else a "Miscellaneous" channel the SDK creates for you — which is where "why is the sound wrong" ends.
- Neither shape reaches a force-stopped or battery-restricted app at all.

Rule of thumb: use a `notification` block only when being rendered by a dead process is the feature — a marketing blast. Anything the product cares about goes data-only, and you own the posting, the routing and the analytics.

An FCM registration token identifies one app instance, not a user and not a device, and it is replaced without warning — if your only upload happens at login, the server keeps paying to notify installs that no longer exist.

### When a token changes
- A fresh install, cleared app data, a restore onto a different device, an explicit `deleteToken()`, and rotation by FCM itself.
- `onNewToken` is your only callback, and it can fire before anyone has signed in — persist it locally and upload once you have a user.
- Firebase's own guidance is to treat a token you have not seen refreshed in roughly two months as stale; an instance that has been silent far longer stops being deliverable.

### What each side owes
1. Client, every launch: read `FirebaseMessaging.getInstance().token` and upload if it differs from the last value you uploaded. `onNewToken` alone is not enough — the process may not have been alive when the token changed.
2. Client, on logout: call `deleteToken()` **and** tell the server to drop the row. Otherwise the next person to sign in on that phone receives the previous user's notifications, which is a privacy incident, not a nit.
3. Server: store token, user id, platform, app version and `updated_at`; delete the row the moment a send returns `UNREGISTERED` or `INVALID_ARGUMENT`; expire rows by `updated_at`.
4. Server: never assume one token per user. One user has several devices, and one device hosts several accounts over its life.

`token` needs Google Play services and returns a `Task` that can fail outright. On a device without them there is no token at all, so the settings screen that says "notifications on" has to reflect that instead of lying.

Nothing should buzz: the message lands in the repository, the open screen updates from it, and one notification presenter — the only thing that knows what is on screen — decides not to post. That decision belongs in the presenter, never scattered through `onMessageReceived`.

### The path
1. `onMessageReceived` writes the message through the repository and does nothing UI-shaped. That part always runs, in every app state.
2. The open screen collects the same Flow and renders the new row. The user watches it arrive; there is no notification to suppress after the fact.
3. The presenter asks two questions: is the app foregrounded (`ProcessLifecycleOwner.get().lifecycle.currentState.isAtLeast(RESUMED)`), and is *this* conversation the visible one — a small app-scoped holder the screen sets on resume and clears on pause.
4. Visible: suppress and mark read. Foregrounded but a different thread: an in-app banner. Backgrounded: post normally.

### The traps
- A `notification`-block message drawn by the system while you are backgrounded cannot be suppressed at all, so chat has to be data-only for any of this to be implementable.
- Opening a thread must cancel its existing notification with `NotificationManagerCompat.cancel(convId)`, and the server should cancel it on the user's other devices with a data-only "read" push.
- Reuse one stable notification id per conversation and set `setOnlyAlertOnce(true)`, so the fifth message updates the notification instead of buzzing a fifth time.
- Do not sniff the current Activity from the service. One holder, written by one lifecycle observer, read in one place.

Mental model: a system notification is how you reach a user who is not looking. If they are looking, the UI is the notification.

A shared `collapse_key` made each of those four messages replace the previous one still sitting in the queue, and normal priority left the driver push waiting for the device's next Doze maintenance window.

### Collapsing and queueing
- `collapse_key` means "supersede any undelivered message with this key for this device". It is right for a state ping — a badge count, a sync cursor — and wrong for anything the user must read, because only the last one survives.
- FCM tracks at most four distinct collapse keys per device and makes no promise about which it keeps once you exceed that.
- Non-collapsible messages queue too, up to about 100 per device. Past that FCM discards the whole queue and delivers a single `onDeletedMessages()` callback, whose only correct handling is a full sync.

### Priority and lifetime
- `android.priority: "high"` wakes a Dozing device and briefly allowlists your process for network access. `normal` waits for the next maintenance window, which on an idle phone in a low standby bucket is measured in hours.
- High priority is metered: FCM watches whether your high-priority messages produce a user-visible notification, and downgrades an app that abuses it. Compare `RemoteMessage.getPriority()` with `getOriginalPriority()` in production to see whether it already has.
- `ttl` is how long FCM may store an undelivered message; the default and the maximum are both four weeks. `ttl: 0` means "deliver right now or throw it away" — correct for an incoming call or a one-time code, which are worthless late.

Choose per message type, not per app: driver-arrived is high priority, a `ttl` of minutes, no collapse key; a chat message is high priority and not collapsible; a badge refresh is normal, collapsible and long-lived.
code_example:
// Server, Firebase Admin SDK. One shape per message type, never one for all.

fun driverArrived(token: String, rideId: String): Message = Message.builder()
  .setToken(token)
  .putData("ride_id", rideId)
  .setAndroidConfig(
    AndroidConfig.builder()
      .setPriority(AndroidConfig.Priority.HIGH)      // wake it out of Doze
      .setTtl(120_000)                               // worthless after two minutes
      .build()                                        // and no collapse key at all
  ).build()

fun chatMessage(token: String, convId: String, msgId: String): Message = Message.builder()
  .setToken(token)
  .putData("conversation_id", convId)
  .putData("message_id", msgId)
  .setAndroidConfig(
    AndroidConfig.builder()
      .setPriority(AndroidConfig.Priority.HIGH)
      // WRONG here: .setCollapseKey("chat-" + convId)
      // four messages sent while the phone dozes -> one delivered
      .build()
  ).build()

fun badgeRefresh(token: String): Message = Message.builder()
  .setToken(token)
  .putData("action", "refresh_badge")
  .setAndroidConfig(
    AndroidConfig.builder()
      .setPriority(AndroidConfig.Priority.NORMAL)    // a maintenance window is fine
      .setCollapseKey("badge")                       // only the newest one matters
      .setTtl(TimeUnit.DAYS.toMillis(1))
      .build()
  ).build()

class AppMessagingService : FirebaseMessagingService() {
  // The device's queue overflowed: everything pending is gone, so resync.
  override fun onDeletedMessages() {
    SyncWorker.enqueueFullSync(this)
  }
}

`USE_FULL_SCREEN_INTENT` became a restricted permission in Android 14: only apps whose core function is calling or alarms are granted it at install, everyone else is denied by default, and a denied full-screen intent silently degrades into an ordinary heads-up notification.

### What the platform actually does
- A full-screen intent was never a guarantee. Since Android 10 it launches its Activity only when the screen is locked or off; otherwise the system shows a heads-up and leaves the user where they are.
- It also needs a channel of `IMPORTANCE_HIGH`. On a lower-importance channel it never fires, permission or not.
- On Android 14+ check `NotificationManager.canUseFullScreenIntent()` and, when it is false, send the user to `Settings.ACTION_MANAGE_APP_USE_FULL_SCREEN_INTENT` for your package. Google Play only grants it at install to apps that declare calling or alarms as their core function, and it reviews that declaration.

### What a call app is expected to look like now
- `NotificationCompat.CallStyle.forIncomingCall(person, declineIntent, answerIntent)` on a high-importance channel, with `setCategory(CATEGORY_CALL)`, `setOngoing(true)`, and the full-screen intent attached as a *request*.
- Back it with a foreground service declared `phoneCall` — Android 14 enforces the type — started inside the temporary allowlist that a high-priority FCM message opens.
- A serious VoIP app registers with `ConnectionService` in self-managed mode, so the system arbitrates audio focus and collisions with cellular calls instead of you.

Rule: treat the heads-up as the normal path and the takeover as an upgrade you might not get. An app that only works with a full-screen intent is broken for every user who said no.

Split the path into segments you can count — accepted by FCM, delivered to the device, posted by your process, opened by the user — because "notifications don't arrive" covers four unrelated failures and only one of them is the OEM's doing.

### Instrument the four segments
1. Server: log the message id every send returns, plus the per-token error for the ones that fail.
2. Delivery: Firebase's Cloud Messaging delivery data, and its BigQuery export for per-message rows, tells you what FCM did — delivered, dropped because the device was inactive, dropped for too many messages, or delayed for the app's standby bucket.
3. Receipt: in `onMessageReceived`, log the message id, the lag against `sentTime`, and `getPriority()` against `getOriginalPriority()` so you can see FCM downgrading you.
4. Posting: immediately before `notify()`, log `areNotificationsEnabled()` and the channel's `importance`. A user who switched that channel off looks identical to a lost push from the server's side, and in most of these tickets that is the whole answer.

### Reproducing it on a device
- `adb shell dumpsys notification --noredact` shows the posted records and channel state; `adb shell am set-standby-bucket <pkg> restricted` and `adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle` reproduce the delayed case with a normal-priority send.
- Report `ActivityManager.isBackgroundRestricted()` and `PowerManager.isIgnoringBatteryOptimizations()` with the receipt event: an aggressive OEM battery manager shows up as a whole cohort with background restriction on.
- A force-stopped app receives nothing until the user launches it again. That is platform behaviour everywhere, not an OEM quirk.

Only then can you act — prompt the affected cohort to exempt the app, or raise priority for the messages that justify it. Without the segments you are guessing.

You control exactly one thing — the notification's visibility and the redacted `setPublicVersion` shown in its place; whether a locked screen shows notifications at all belongs to the user's lock settings and, on a managed device, to the admin.

### What visibility means
- `VISIBILITY_PUBLIC` shows the notification in full on the lock screen. `VISIBILITY_PRIVATE` substitutes your `setPublicVersion` or, if you never supplied one, a generic "Contents hidden" line that reads like a bug. `VISIBILITY_SECRET` keeps it off the lock screen entirely.
- It only applies to a secure lock — PIN, pattern, password — and only while the user has not chosen to show all notification content. The channel carries its own `setLockscreenVisibility`, applied at creation and the user's to change afterwards; a per-notification value cannot exceed the channel's.
- None of it touches the heads-up on an unlocked phone, which is where a code is most often read over a shoulder. Keep the digits out of the title, and add `setTimeoutAfter` so the notification expires with the code.

### The parts you do not own
- Since Android 15 the platform detects one-time codes itself and redacts them from notification listeners that lack the restricted `RECEIVE_SENSITIVE_NOTIFICATIONS` permission. Treat it as a backstop — it is heuristic and version-gated, so set your own visibility anyway.
- In a work profile the admin can force every notification to be redacted through `setKeyguardDisabledFeatures` with `KEYGUARD_DISABLE_UNREDACTED_NOTIFICATIONS`, and when the profile is paused its notifications disappear entirely — so a work-profile user reporting nothing arriving may simply have work mode off.

Rule of thumb: build the public version as a real, useful notification with the same tap target, not a placeholder. Then the strict setting costs the user nothing.
